---
title: "Expected and state-specific reporting loss"
subtitle: "3.11 · after the postrank theory book, ch. 16–18 and vignette m2"
description: "Comparison of minimum expected loss with realized losses in paired posterior draws."
---

A report that minimizes posterior expected loss can lose to another report in many individual states. This
comparison keeps both reports fixed and evaluates them on the same posterior states. The frequency with which
the comparison report has lower loss and the average difference in loss answer different questions. The
finite-state example gives both quantities exactly. The simulations show how estimates of those quantities
vary across samples.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Inside the family.** Among 63 reports with at most two grades, the best has conditional risk .0940; the two
  posterior-mean tiers have .1046. Yet that common rule wins 57 of these 100 paired draws. The difference in loss can be large even when the common rule wins more often. Points below the dashed diagonal
  show states where the common rule has lower loss.
- **Outside the family.** The comparison retains the two-grade family but uses a three-tier comparator. Its conditional
  risk .0417 is below .0940. The search still allows only two grades, so its minimum applies only to reports in that family.
- **Two-state law.** The best report withholds at risk .2500; the expected-rank order has risk .3000. Nevertheless
  the rule wins with exact probability .700 and wins 65 of these 100 sampled draws. The state table gives the exact probabilities and losses. The scatter shows the sampled outcomes.
- **A short run.** The rule wins 9 of 10 draws, and the paired mean difference is −.00667, favoring it in this
  finite sample. The exact conditional difference is positive; the paired Monte Carlo SE quantifies numerical sampling variation.
- **A silent common rule.** Its risk is .2000 and its disclosed-error fraction is “NA: no disclosure.” Silence
  costs τ per pair, so a report that states nothing does not have zero reporting loss.
- **Identical reports.** The summary reads “ties 100”: both reports have the same loss in every drawn state.
  Draw selection gives the corresponding state, grades and wrong counts.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Reporting loss adds wrong stated directions and withholding costs and divides the sum by all pairs. The wrong
fraction uses stated pairs as its denominator. The minimum expected loss applies to reports in the search under
the given posterior and loss. The paired standard error measures how the estimated difference varies across
posterior samples. The model is fixed throughout.
:::
